sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: The honor-price is an ancient Irish legal tradition. The Irish name is eric. The law set a payment, or eric, for a crime, scaled to the victim's rank. Celtic Ireland had no police and no court system. Instead, each person held an honor-price set by rank. The debt came due on murder or injury done to the tuath, the tribe. If one man killed another, the killer and his kin owed an eric of gold, cattle, slaves, and other goods to the victim's kin. The terms rose with the victim's rank. Other wrongs, such as slander and rape, also drew an eric. The whole kinship group shared the debt, so the law curbed the hotblooded young. Many Irish myths turn on collecting an honor-price. The Sons of Tuireann had to perform impossible feats to pay off the eric for killing their father's enemy Cian. The Senchas Mor, the great book of law, stated that every eric is evil, for the debt almost always led to yet more bloodshed.
